topic: The Binary Secret of the Tower of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students and early undergraduate computer science students

outline.topic: The Binary Secret of the Tower of Hanoi
outline.target_audience: High school students and early undergraduate computer science students

sections.title: The Puzzle Setup: Rules of the Game
sections.content: Introduce the Tower of Hanoi components: three vertical pegs and a stack of 'n' disks of different sizes. Explain the two core rules: 1. Only one disk can be moved at a time. 2. A larger disk can never be placed on top of a smaller disk. Establish the goal: move the entire stack to a different peg in the minimum number of moves.
sections.example: A curious robot named 'Alpha' is trying to move 3 golden pancakes from Peg A to Peg C without ever squashing a smaller pancake.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Binary Counting as a Pulse
sections.content: Visualize binary counting as a sequence of bits flipping. Explain that in a binary number, each position (bit) represents a power of 2. Show a 3-bit counter (000 to 111) and highlight which specific bit changes during each increment. Use a 'lightbulb' graphic where 'Off' is 0 and 'On' is 1.
sections.example: Sequence: 000 -> 001 (Bit 1 flips) -> 010 (Bit 1 and 2 flip) -> 011 (Bit 1 flips). Notice that Bit 1 flips every 1 step, Bit 2 every 2 steps, and Bit 3 every 4 steps.

sections.title: The Mapping: Disks as Bits
sections.content: Create a one-to-one mapping between the binary bits and the disks. Disk 1 (smallest) corresponds to the rightmost bit (2^0). Disk 2 corresponds to the second bit (2^1), and so on. Explain the 'Magic Rule': Whenever a bit in the binary counter changes its value (0 to 1 or 1 to 0), the corresponding disk must be moved.
sections.example: In a 3-disk game, counting from 0 to 7 in binary (000 to 111) provides the exact timing for every move. When the counter goes from 000 to 001, Bit 1 changes, so we move Disk 1.

sections.title: The Directional Logic: Where to Move?
sections.content: Explain the spatial logic using a cyclic movement pattern. For an odd number of disks: move the smallest disk in the cycle A -> C -> B -> A. For an even number: A -> B -> C -> A. All other disks move to the only available legal position. This ensures the binary 'flip' always results in a valid move.
sections.example: Graphic: A triangular path showing Pegs A, B, and C. When the binary counter hits '001', Disk 1 (the smallest) follows the arrow from A to C.

sections.title: Synthesis: Solving the 3-Disk Puzzle
sections.content: Walk through the full 7-step solution ($2^3 - 1$) by incrementing the binary counter. Show a split-screen: left side increments binary (001, 010, 011...), right side animates the corresponding disk move. Emphasize that the 'rightmost changed bit' always identifies the disk to be moved.
sections.example: At Step 4 (binary 100), the 3rd bit is the rightmost bit that changed from the previous state (011). Therefore, we move Disk 3 (the largest).

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of 2^n - 1
sections.content: Summarize why binary counting is the perfect mathematical model for this recursive problem. Introduce the formula for total moves: $M = 2^n - 1$. Explain that the binary representation of the move number tells you exactly which disk is currently in motion.
sections.example: If you had 64 disks like the Monks in the original legend, the binary counter would reach a number with 64 ones, taking $2^{64}-1$ moves—roughly 585 billion years!

storyboard.title: The Puzzle Setup: Rules of the Game
lecture_lines: The Tower of Hanoi has three pegs and disks.
Rule one: move only one disk at a time.
Rule two: no larger disk atop a smaller one.
Goal: move the stack to a different peg.
Binary counting reveals the most efficient solution.
animations: Show three pegs labeled A, B, and C with 3 disks stacked on A.
Animate the top disk (Disk 1) moving from Peg A to Peg B.
Try to move Disk 2 on top of Disk 1; flash red #FF0000 to indicate an invalid move.
Move Disk 2 to Peg C, showing a valid move following the rules.
Highlight the entire stack on Peg A and the empty Peg C as the target.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Binary Counting as a Pulse
lecture_lines: Binary counting uses a sequence of flipping bits.
Each bit position represents a power of two.
Observe which bit flips during each increment.
animations: Display binary '000' in white #FFFFFF at the center.
Transition '000' to '001', highlighting the rightmost bit in yellow #FFFF00.
Transition '001' to '010', highlighting the middle bit in green #00FF00.
Display three lightbulbs; the first one toggles 'On' and 'Off' with each count increment.
The second lightbulb toggles every 2 counts, and the third every 4 counts.

storyboard.title: The Mapping: Disks as Bits
lecture_lines: Map each disk to a specific binary bit.
The smallest disk corresponds to the rightmost bit.
Second disk maps to the second binary bit.
The largest disk maps to the third bit.
Move the disk when its bit changes value.
animations: Align 'Disk 1', 'Disk 2', and 'Disk 3' vertically with bits '2^0', '2^1', and '2^2'.
Simultaneously flash the first bit and Disk 1 in magenta #FF00FF.
Show the counter change 000 to 001 and move Disk 1 to indicate the mapping.

storyboard.title: The Directional Logic: Where to Move?
lecture_lines: Move disks in a consistent cyclic pattern.
Odd total: move the smallest disk A-C-B-A.
Even total: move the smallest disk A-B-C-A.
animations: Draw Pegs A, B, and C in a triangle with clockwise arrows A to C to B.
Label the path 'Odd n = 3' and highlight the A to C arrow.
Move Disk 1 from Peg A to Peg C following the highlighted arrow.

storyboard.title: Synthesis: Solving the 3-Disk Puzzle
lecture_lines: Increment the binary counter to identify each move.
The rightmost bit flip determines which disk moves.
Step four flips the third bit for the largest disk.
Follow the sequence to reach the final state.
Seven moves complete the three-disk puzzle.
animations: Create a split-screen with 'Binary Counter' on left and 'Towers' on right.
Binary increments from '011' to '100'; highlight the changed 3rd bit in cyan #00FFFF.
Move Disk 3 from Peg A to Peg B on the right side of the screen.
Sequence through the remaining steps quickly until the counter reaches '111'.
All disks are now stacked on Peg C; the screen glows gold #FFD700.

storyboard.title: Conclusion: The Power of 2^n - 1
lecture_lines: Binary counting perfectly models the Tower of Hanoi.
Total moves equal two to the power n minus one.
Each move is encoded in the binary sequence.
animations: Display the formula 'M = 2^n - 1' in large cyan #00FFFF text.
Show n = 64 and the resulting massive number of moves below it.
Text '585 Billion Years' appears and slowly scales up in white #FFFFFF.
